newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia agrees on central bank, currency - officials.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia agrees on central bank, currency - officials.

text.p: Bosnia's Serb, Croat and Moslem leaders agreed on Tuesday to form a single central bank and an interim currency with different designs for each of its two territories, U.S. and Bosnian officials said.

After months of haggling, Serb leaders dropped a demand for two central banks for the first time and accepted the central bank concept set out under a peace treaty, said Mirza Hajric, aide to the chairman of the collective presidency.
As a concession to the Serbs it was agreed that an interim bank note, called a "convertible coupon", will be issued with different designs, Hajric told Reuters.
"The concession was in the design issue, but the essence -- that it is to be used throughout Bosnia -- is more important," Hajric said.
The convertible coupons, pegged at parity to the German mark, will be issued by one central bank and will not bear the names of Bosnia's two entities, the Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic.
"The differences are in pictures, but they will not bear nationalist symbols, just some pictures acceptable to everyone," Hajric said.
He said an acceptable design had not yet been agreed but said he did not expect the design issue to present a problem.
Political leaders are under pressure to adopt a central bank law, of which the currency is only one issue, to clear the way for an international fund-raising conference for reconstruction.

The donors conference has already been postponed twice since its original March date because the inter-ethnic government has failed to pass a set of economic reform laws required by the international community before the conference.

Bosnia also needs to clinch a deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) which wants to see a functioning central bank and budget laws adopted before the conference, likely to be held at the end of May in Brussels.
"With this solution (interim currency) we shall establish a unified payment system in Bosnia-Herzegovina," Hajric said.
The convertible coupons will take up to three months to be printed and are expected to be in use about one year, until Bosnia's proper, permanent currency is agreed.
The agreement, announced after talks attended by U.S. envoy John Kornblum, must be approved as part of the central bank law by an inter-ethnic parliament.
The presidency members agreed on the name of future single currency, the convertible mark or "marka" in Bosnian, but left other issues unresolved.
"So far, there is only an agreement on the future currency's name -- convertible mark -- but not on its design.
"We shall insist that the interim solution does not grow into a permanent one," Hajric said.
The Dayton peace agreement, signed in December 1995, calls for a single central bank operating for six years as a currency board.
Under the treaty, the currency board rules stipulate that the central bank can only issue Bosnian currency backed by hard currency reserves.
